name: Creating a List of Words from a File
description: Construct a program that reads a text file and creates a list of the words that the file contains, ignoring the case of the letters. Assume that all of the words in the text file are separated by a single space characters.

comments.content: This statement creates a JVocabulary1 object using the new keyword and empty parentheses. The variable v1 holds a reference to a JVocabulary1 object.

We need to read the file and create a list of words that the file contains. This statement invokes the method getWords of the v1 and passes the file name "test1.txt" as its argument. This method returns a reference to the list of words. We assign this reference to variable lst.
This statement prints the list by showing the contents of the list inside square brackets, with the values separated by commas.

Note that we can print the content of an ArrayList because the ArrayList class overrides Java’s toString method. The toString method is called when we print an ArrayList or concatenate an ArrayList to a String.

We need to declare the method that creates an ArrayList of words that the given file contains. We define this method as public to provide access to this method from outside of the class. Also, we define its return type as ArrayList of String, as it returns an ArrayList that holds String values.

We need to have a list that could store String values because each word is a String. The following statement creates an empty ArrayList for storing Strings and assigns its reference to variable words. We use ArrayList instead of an array because arrays have fixed length while ArrayList is dynamic in size. In situations like this that we don't know the maximum number of elements that we have to process, we need to use ArrayList. As elements are added to an ArrayList its capacity grows automatically.
The try blocks tries to execute the code within it. The statements in the try block may throw several types of exception.
If an error is encountered, the try block code execution is stopped and transferred down to the catch block(s).

We want to read a text file; therefore, we need to use a FileReader and wrap it in a BufferedReader. This statement create a FileReader object using the new keyword and empty parentheses. The variable fr holds a reference to a FileReader object.
We wrap a BufferedReader around the FileReader because the BufferedReader buffers the input to make the reading process much faster. The variable br holds a reference to a BufferedReader object.
We define a string variable to hold the content of each line that the BufferedReader object reads from the file. We set it to null.

We need to read the lines as long as we have not reached the end of the file. Therefore, we need to use a loop structure. Since we don't know ahead of time how many times the loop will be repeated, we need to use a while loop. The condition in the while loop tests whether the body of the loop should be repeated, so it should test whether the line that is read is not null.

We could read a line by invoking the readLine method of the BufferedReader object. Here, we compare the result of calling the readLine method to null. We assign the result of calling the readLine method to variable line because we need to process it in the body of the while loop.
The body of the while loop is repeated as long as the line that is read is not null. The loop terminates when the loop condition evaluates to false, that is when the line that is read is null.
We need to split the line into words and store the words in an array. We don’t care about capitalization, so we convert the line to lowecase before splitting it into words.

We convert the string characters into lowercase by calling the method toLowerCase on that string. We use split() method with " " as its argument because we want the split method to separate strings using a single space character.

We use a for loop to iterate over the words and add each word to the ArrayList. We can do this by using for–each statement that visits each word in the array of line tokens. This for loop assigns the name token to each of the values in the array in turn, from left to right, and then the statement in the loop body will be executed for each value.
This method adds the word that we visited to the end of the list.
We can add an element to the ArrayList by calling the add() method.

We're done reading the file; so, we need to close the BufferedReader object. Closing a BufferedReader object will also close the Reader object from which the BufferedReader is reading. Therefore, we don't need to close the FileReader object (i.e., object referred by variable fr) when the BufferedReader object is closed .
This statement prints to the default standard output stream the error that caused the FileNotFoundException. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
We need to handle the IOException. This error occurs when an error occurs when trying to read/close the file.
The body of this catch block gets executed only if an error occurs when trying to read/close the file. Otherwise, the body of this catch statement is skipped.
This statement prints to the default standard output stream the error that caused the IOException. The printed text is followed by the end-of-line character at the end.
Now that we processed the file, we need to return the list of words that the file contains. The return statement, when reached, ends the method call and sends the result back to the caller.
